item.subject: Mathematics
item.stem:
Chris has lots of tiles like this: [Image: Chris's tile]

Julio has lots of tiles like this: [Image: Julio's tile]

Pierre has lots of tiles like this: [Image: Pierre's tile]

Ben has lots of tiles like this: [Image: Ben's tile]

Who would need the least number of tiles to cover a classroom floor with his tiles?
item.figure_description:
Four rectangular/square outlines representing tiles, each shown to the right of a person's name:
- Chris's tile: a medium-small square.
- Julio's tile: a large horizontal rectangle, with both width and area visibly greater than all the other tiles.
- Pierre's tile: a small square, noticeably smaller than Chris's.
- Ben's tile: a medium-large square, larger than Chris's and Pierre's, but smaller in area than Julio's rectangle.
item.calibration: Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2003 data, 2007 bridging data, and 2007 data (fourth-grade mathematics).

reference_items.stem:
[Image: Three arrangements of 3 tiles labeled Rita, Ina, and Lana]

Rita, Ina, and Lana take turns arranging 3 tiles. Each arranges the tiles in a different shape as shown above. Which of the following is true about the area of the shapes?

options.label: A
options.text: Rita’s shape has a greater area than the others.

options.label: B
options.text: Ina’s shape has a greater area than the others.

options.label: C
options.text: Lana’s shape has a greater area than the others.

options.label: D
options.text: All of the shapes have the same area.

reference_items.figure_description:
Three arrangements of three tiles each, labeled "Rita", "Ina", and "Lana":
- Rita: Two squares are placed side by side horizontally, sharing a vertical edge. A triangle sits on top of the left square, with its base along the top edge of that square and its apex pointing upward.
- Ina: A square sits at the top with horizontal top and bottom edges. Attached below it is a triangle sharing the square's bottom horizontal edge and pointing downward. Attached to the lower-right edge of the triangle is a second square, tilted diagonally downward and to the right.
- Lana: Two squares are placed side by side horizontally, sharing a vertical edge. Attached to the right vertical edge of the right square is a triangle pointing to the right.

reference_items.figure_description:
At the top is an equilateral triangle with dots at each of its three vertices, labeled "tile" to the right of its right edge.

Below is an irregular polygon drawn on an isometric (triangular) dot grid, with dots marking vertices along its boundary and in its interior:
- Top edge: a horizontal segment 3 units long, with 4 dots evenly spaced (including endpoints).
- Left boundary: from the top-left dot, a line goes down and right by 1 unit to an indented vertex dot; from there, a line goes down and left by 1 unit to the bottom-left corner dot.
- Bottom edge: a horizontal segment 4 units long, with 5 dots evenly spaced (including endpoints).
- Right boundary: from the top-right dot, a line goes down and right by 1 unit to a vertex dot at the middle horizontal level; from that dot, a horizontal line extends right by 1 unit to another vertex dot; from that dot, a line goes down and left by 1 unit to the bottom-right corner dot.
- Interior: 2 dots are spaced along the middle horizontal level between the left indented vertex and the right boundary.

Combinations of the numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4. Every number is used only once.
Combinations of the numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4. One or more numbers are used more than once.
Combinations containing one or more numbers other than 1, 2, 3 and 4
Other incorrect

Instruction:

For this item, you have been given a piece of cardboard with 6 tiles like the ones shown below. Take the piece of cardboard, and punch out the 6 tiles.

If you do not have the piece of cardboard, raise your hand.

4 Triangle Tiles
[Image: Four triangle tiles]

2 Trapezoid Tiles
[Image: Two trapezoid tiles]

These tiles can be used to make new figures. One problem has been done for you

USE: 3 Triangle Tiles
MAKE: A trapezoid
SHOW: Draw it on the grid.
[Image: Example showing a trapezoid drawn on the grid]

Now try these problems.

B.

SHOW: Draw it on the grid.

[Image: Triangular grid]

descriptors:
Makes a correct 6-sided figure, e.g., one of those shown below (in any orientation).
[Image: Five sample 6-sided figures each made from two trapezoid tiles: a regular hexagon joined at the long bases; an hourglass shape joined at the short bases; an L-shaped figure joined along legs; an offset hexagon joined partially along long bases; and another 6-sided figure joined along legs]

Blank

reference_items.figure_description:
The stem includes four diagrams:
1. '4 Triangle Tiles': Four identical equilateral triangles of unit side length, arranged in a row pointing alternately up, down, up, and down.
2. '2 Trapezoid Tiles': Two identical isosceles trapezoids each composed of three equilateral triangle units (bottom base 2 units, top base 1 unit, legs 1 unit for the first one; and inverted with top base 2 units, bottom base 1 unit for the second one).
3. Worked example grid: An isometric grid forming a parallelogram with horizontal top and bottom sides of 3 units each and slanted sides of 2 units each, divided by dashed lines into 2 rows of 6 equilateral triangles. In the top-right portion, a trapezoid made of 3 triangle units (top side 1 unit, bottom side 2 units, slanted sides 1 unit) is outlined in bold solid lines.
4. Part B response grid: An identical empty parallelogram-shaped isometric grid with top and bottom edges of 3 units, slanted sides of 2 units, divided into 2 rows of 6 equilateral triangle units by dashed lines.

| Name | Savings |
| :--- | :--- |

reference_items.figure_description:
Four bar graphs labeled A, B, C, and D. Each graph has a vertical axis labeled "Savings (in zeds)" marked from 0 to 25 in increments of 5 with horizontal grid lines, and a horizontal axis with four labeled bars: Sara, Peter, Pamela, and Chris.
- In Graph A: Sara's bar height is about 22, Peter's bar height is 15, Pamela's bar height is about 17, and Chris's bar height is 10.
- In Graph B: Sara's bar height is about 22, Peter's bar height is about 17, Pamela's bar height is 15, and Chris's bar height is 10.
- In Graph C: Sara's bar height is about 22, Peter's bar height is 10, Pamela's bar height is 15, and Chris's bar height is about 17.
- In Graph D: Sara's bar height is about 17, Peter's bar height is 15, Pamela's bar height is about 22, and Chris's bar height is 10.

slope.instructions: TIMSS scaled this 1-point item with the three-parameter logistic (3PL) model, which TIMSS uses for multiple-choice items, in the calibration "Concurrent calibration of the TIMSS 2003 data, 2007 bridging data, and 2007 data (fourth-grade mathematics)". What is the item's slope (discrimination) parameter a? A higher a means that the item separates students of lower and higher mathematics ability more sharply. Choose the value closest to it. The state also lists reference items: the calibrated TIMSS items of the same grade most similar to this one (never the item itself or its other parts), most similar first, with their percent correct and their calibrated parameters, each on the scale of its own calibration. Use them to place this item.
